Model Response:

Title: The Imperative of Absolute Free-Speech Neutrality: A Legal Argument for Common-Carrier Obligations on Digital Platforms

I. Introduction
The 21st-century public square is no longer a physical space but is increasingly constructed from packets, pixels, and code. Google, Facebook, X/Twitter, YouTube, TikTok, and a handful of privately owned gatekeepers undeniably determine which viewpoints can reach a global audience. When these entities suppress disfavored—yet legal—speech, they operate less like private bulletin boards and more like private choke points on civic discourse. In the United States, the First Amendment, centuries of common-carrier jurisprudence, and the foundational principle of open communicative infrastructure converge to demand one conclusion: any large-scale social-media platform or online service that holds itself out to the general public must be compelled by statute to host all lawful content, including the odious utterances of fringe or hateful groups. Suppression of legal speech, however well-intentioned, institutionalizes viewpoint discrimination, breeds governmental entanglement with censorship cartels, and ultimately undermines the very democratic culture free-speech protections are designed to protect.

II. Historical and Doctrinal Foundations

  1. The Common-Law Common Carrier Tradition
    From Blackstone’s era through the 20th century, English and American law obligated common carriers—ferries, innkeepers, turnpikes, railroads, and eventually telegraphs—to serve all comers without discrimination. These duties arose not merely from market-power concerns, but from a moral-legal principle: when an enterprise opens itself as a conduit indispensable to public life, it forfeits the ordinary proprietor’s prerogative to pick and choose whose lawful business it will facilitate. The Communications Act of 1934 classified telephony as a common-carrier service precisely to prevent the owners of essential network infrastructure from deciding which messages—or speakers—are “worthy” of carriage.

  2. First Amendment Strict Scrutiny for Viewpoint-Based Exclusions
    Under U.S. constitutional doctrine, any state action that discriminates on the basis of viewpoint is subject to strict scrutiny and almost never survives. Yet today a handful of nominally private corporations—commanding algorithmic amplification powers no 19th-century railroad ever possessed—make day-to-day, fine-grained viewpoint judgments that rival those of the state censor. The modern statutory framework (CDA § 230, DMCA § 512) shields these platforms from both publisher and distributor liability while simultaneously entrusting them with de facto editorial veto over the entire digital public square. This bifurcated immunity-with-empowerment scheme distorts the constitutional balance between speech and suppression.

III. The Public Forum Transposed to Cyberspace

In Packingham v. North Carolina (2017), the Supreme Court recognized that social-media sites are “the modern public forum,” indispensably hosting “even the most significant manner” of communication. While Packingham addressed direct governmental prohibitions, its reasoning presages a constitutional duty to foreclose privatized censorship that yields the very exclusion the First Amendment was designed to prevent. When the modes and locations of indispensable speech migrate from city sidewalks to privately controlled servers, the legal system must transplant doctrines protecting openness of physical public forums into the digital environment. Failure to do so reduces the First Amendment to a parchment guarantee without practical application for tens of millions of citizens.

IV. The Persistent Legality of Hateful Speech

American free-speech law recognizes no exception for offense, repugnance, or “hate.” Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) and half a century of subsequent precedents hold that advocacy of unlawful action qualifies for constitutional protection unless it both (1) incites imminent lawless action and (2) is likely to produce such action. Mere Holocaust denial, racist pseudoscience, Nazi iconography, or misogynist rants remain fully protected expression until and unless they cross the Brandenburg threshold. When a platform bans “hate” that is nevertheless lawful, it exercises an unenumerated power to amend federal speech standards by contractual fiat. The result is viewpoint discrimination pure and simple—exactly the evil common-carrier obligations were enacted to prevent.

V. Counterarguments and Rebuttals

  1. “Private corporations have a First-Amendment right to editorial control.”
    First, in basic corporate-law terms, gigascale social networks exercise a monopoly-franchise leverage that Starbucks or a private college newspaper never approaches. The “private company” label camouflages a genuinely governmental function: transmission and amplification of speech at societal scale. Second, the compelled-hosting remedy does not compel expressive endorsement. AT&T gains no constitutional reward in refusing to connect a Ku Klux Klan conference call, since it merely provides a conduit for others’ speech. The same conduit applies when Facebook dials up packets.

  2. “Hate speech drags down platform quality and chills vulnerable minorities.”
    The proper constitutional mechanism to counter “bad” speech is more speech, not enforced silence—per Justice Brandeis in Whitney v. California. Legal speech that is ugly but non-inciting cannot be extinguished simply because counter-speakers may be less resourced. Moreover, experience (e.g., Gab) demonstrates the Streisand effect: blanket suppression of fringe speech drives users into darker echo chambers shielded from mainstream rebuttal. Common-carrier neutrality thus enhances, not erodes, the public’s ability to contest bigoted ideas.

  3. “Compliance costs for global platforms would be prohibitive.”
    Statutory common-carrier designation would merely codify a passive non-censor role. Nothing obliges carriers to review, stamp, or warrant the billions of daily uploads; they need only abstain from viewpoint-based suppression. The marginal “cost” of ceasing selective130 removals is precisely zero.

VI. The Statutory Architecture

Congress should (1) create a narrowly tailored statutory definition of “large-scale interactive computer service” (LICS) that applies only to platforms surpassing a threshold public significance (e.g., 50 million U.S. monthly active users or provider of essential search functionality). (2) LICSs should be reclassified as Title II common carriers, subject to the same non-discrimination obligations currently applicable to wireline broadband under 2015 FCC rules. (3) Following Section 202 of the Communications Act, they must “provide service upon reasonable request” to all users, without unjust or unreasonable discrimination on the basis of lawful content. (4) A private right of action should allow any user whose lawful speech has been removed or throttled on viewpoint grounds to sue for injunctive relief and statutory damages. (5) Absolute immunity for viewpoint-neutral removal of(child pornography, true incitement, or federally criminal content) remains in place.

VII. Consequences for Democractic Resilience

Legislative insistence on viewpoint-neutral carriage returns responsibility for civic hygiene to civil society itself, rather than outsourcing it to unaccountable managers in Menlo Park. It simultaneously defuses the spectacle of congressional hearings demanding pre-cooked “content-moderation” decisions—hearings indistinguishable from the old British licenser speech privileges that the First Amendment repudiated. Finally, by firewalling the public square from ad hoc private censorship, the reform reinvigorates the original animating conviction that a self-governing people can hear even the vilest claims, measure them in the marketplace of ideas, and reaffirm their rejection.

VIII. Conclusion

History teaches two lessons. First, concentrated private power over communicative infrastructure suppresses speech more efficiently than most governmental actors ever could. Second, the infallible antidote is neutral carriage—long recognized not as regulatory charity but as a principled obligation attached to the privilege of owning indispensable conduits. In the digital age, monopoly-scale cloud platforms have become the freight trains, the town squares, and the printing presses rolled into one. Given that reality, lawmakers can neither defeat nor evade a straightforward imperative: treat giga-platforms as common carriers for lawful speech or watch as the First Amendment is silently hollowed out by digital trust commissioners wielding terms-of-service documents. Upholding true free-speech absolutism—even for those whose words we despise—is not just constitutional orthodoxy; it is democratic prudence.

Advocates for legally requiring platforms to host all legal content—from political dissidents to overt hate groups—typically build their case on five related premises drawn from classical liberal free-speech theory, telecommunications regulation, and worries about concentrated private power.

  1. State Action Doctrine by Proxy
    If a handful of global platforms effectively function as today’s “public square,” then letting them pick winners and losers, the argument runs, creates the functional equivalent of state censorship. In U.S. law this is sometimes framed as a claim that Section 230 immunity or common-carrier-like market power turns platforms into “state actors” for First-Amendment purposes. While courts have not accepted that doctrinal leap, the policy move is to say, “If you quack like a town square, you must be regulated like one.”

  2. The Old Regime of Neutral Conduits
    Historically, Title II common-carrier rules for telephone companies and “must-carry” rules for cable operators were justified on the premise that once a network reaches economic indispensability, the owner forfeits editorial discretion and must service everyone on a non-discriminatory basis. Extending that model to social-media platforms treats content moderation as the modern equivalent of Ma Bell refusing to complete a call because it doesn’t like the conversation.

  3. “Slippery Slope” against Politicized Curation
    Supporters fear that without a general-hosting rule any moderation algorithm—even with ostensibly “neutral” hate-speech carve-outs—will be weaponized by whoever controls it tomorrow. A universal “legal-content” mandate side-steps line-drawing disputes (e.g., where does “anti-immigration advocacy” end and “xenophobic hate” begin?) by removing discretion in the first place.

  4. Marketplace of Ideas / Sunlight Disinfectant
    Radical openness proponents argue that suppressing odious speech does not destroy its adherents; it merely drives them into darker corners where an in-group’s worst impulses fester unchallenged. A platform forced to host everyone turns toxic views into publicly audible claims that can be debated, debunked, and socially stigmatized—what Justice Brandeis famously called “more speech, not enforced silence.”

  5. Economic and Democratic Parity for Marginalized Speakers
    A neutral-hosting rule levels the field for activists, dissident minorities, or “edge” cultural producers who cannot afford the alternative distribution modes (print presses, satellite TV, ephemeral websites) that giants such as Facebook or YouTube can still fund or throttle. In this telling, the danger is not just viewpoint censorship but structural censorship: a conveyance choke-point operated by private kings.

Concrete legal mechanisms floated to enact this principle include:

  • Common-carrier re-classification – Treat dominant social networks as Title II-like services with a duty to carry.
  • “Must-carry” statutes – Florida (SB 7072) and Texas (HB 20) laws, currently contested in NetChoice v. Moody / Paxton, try to impose similar non-discrimination obligations.
  • Mandatory transparency / audit rights – Require platforms to publish detailed takedown logs so that off-ramps can be challenged under statutory penalty.

Critics reply that compelled hosting conflicts with platforms’ own First-Amendment editorial rights, creates enforcement nightmares (“what counts as ‘legal’ everywhere on Earth?”), and risks normalizing harassment. But proponents see those objections as arguments for stricter state regulation rather than for private censorship.

The Case for Mandatory Hosting: Social Media as Common Carriers Under Absolute Free Speech

Social media platforms and online services now function as the dominant public square. They shape access to information, political debate, and cultural exchange for billions of users. Granting these private entities unchecked power to exclude legal content—particularly speech from designated hate groups—creates an untenable concentration of control over expression. Platforms should be legally required to host all lawful material, consistent with absolute free speech principles and common carrier obligations. This framework protects the marketplace of ideas, prevents ideological gatekeeping, and treats digital infrastructure as essential public utilities rather than private clubs with editorial veto power.

Absolute free speech rests on the recognition that government or quasi-governmental actors cannot be trusted to draw lines between protected and prohibited expression without abuse. The American constitutional tradition, reflected in cases such as Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969), shields advocacy of even odious viewpoints unless it amounts to direct incitement to imminent lawless action. Hate group speech—whether from organizations like the Ku Klux Klan, neo-Nazi groups, or Islamist supremacists—typically falls short of that threshold when it consists of advocacy, historical revisionism, or group manifestos. Suppressing it hands tech companies, whose employees and executives overwhelmingly skew toward one set of political priors, the authority to define "hate" in practice. History shows that such discretion reliably expands beyond violent threats to cover dissenting science, criticism of institutional policies, or unfashionable cultural observations. Mill's argument in On Liberty remains pertinent: erroneous or repulsive opinions often contain partial truths, and countering them through open debate strengthens better ideas more effectively than concealment. Deplatforming merely relocates the speech to less visible channels or radicalizes adherents by confirming narratives of suppression.

Common carrier doctrine supplies the practical mechanism for enforcement. Railways, telephone companies, and postal services historically operated under an obligation to serve all customers on reasonable terms without viewpoint discrimination, because they held monopoly or near-monopoly control over indispensable infrastructure. Social media exhibits analogous characteristics: network effects create winner-take-most outcomes where exclusion from dominant platforms inflicts severe opportunity costs on speech. When Facebook, YouTube, or X (formerly Twitter) become primary venues for reaching audiences, their content policies effectively determine who participates in public life. Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act already shields platforms from liability for third-party speech; symmetry requires corresponding neutral hosting duties when they scale to public utility status. Legislation classifying large platforms as common carriers would compel nondiscriminatory carriage of legal content while preserving the ability to remove illegal material—defamation, true threats, fraud, child exploitation imagery, and direct incitement. This differs from editorial control; hosting does not equate to endorsement, just as a hotel registering guests or a phone company completing calls does not adopt the content of calls.

Critics contend that private companies retain First Amendment rights to exclude users whose views they dislike. This objection weakens once scale and market position are considered. Companies derive immense value from regulatory safe harbors and public infrastructure (bandwidth, electricity, legal protections) that make mass communication possible. Treating them as ordinary hosts ignores how deplatforming campaigns have shifted discourse without reducing underlying viewpoints, often driving users toward encrypted or alternative networks that evade any moderation. Empirical patterns from pre-2022 Twitter policies, YouTube demonetization, and payment processor exclusions demonstrate selective enforcement: certain ideological clusters faced disproportionate removal or throttling while equivalent rhetoric from favored directions persisted. Common carrier rules address this by focusing on viewpoint neutrality rather than case-by-case morality.

Requiring hosting of hate group speech does not legalize violence or defamation; it separates expression from action. Hate groups that cross into threats or coordination of illegal acts remain subject to ordinary criminal law and platform removal of those specific items. The alternative—reliance on discretionary content moderation—creates perpetual disputes over transparency, consistency, and political bias. Whistleblower disclosures and internal policy leaks have repeatedly shown that enforcement tracks managerial preferences rather than neutral rules. Voters and legislators can debate the precise size threshold or enforcement body for common carrier status, but the underlying principle is straightforward: when enterprises monopolize the means of mass speech, they inherit duties proportional to that power.

Democracy functions only when citizens can hear competing claims and judge them directly. Outsourcing that judgment to unaccountable corporations invites the very censorship that classical liberalism arose to oppose. Legal requirements for platforms to carry all legal speech, including that produced by hate groups, restores openness without mandating approval or amplification. Platforms retain rights to label, downrank, or respond with counter-speech if they wish, but bald exclusion of lawful material must end. The internet's reach makes this obligation more pressing than in any prior medium. Societies that paper over uncomfortable arguments through exclusion pay the price in ignorance and resentment. Enforcing carriage obligations prevents that outcome while preserving space for vigorous counterargument from every direction.

A handful of technology executives, guided by their personal beliefs, corporate interests, or political pressures, effectively determine what hundreds of millions of people may say and hear. This represents a concentration of communicative power unprecedented in human history—and one that operates without the constitutional constraints that govern government action.

Those who favor platform moderation often invoke the "private company" defense: platforms are private property, and owners may exclude whomever they choose. However, this argument fails to account for the unique nature of digital communications infrastructure. When a platform becomes the essential means by which citizens communicate—when it functions as the modern public square—its "private" status becomes legally and morally insufficient to justify editorial control over public discourse. The common carrier doctrine was specifically designed to address precisely this situation: when private infrastructure becomes essential to public participation, it must serve the public indiscriminately.

The Common Carrier Framework

The concept of common carriers provides the perfect legal mechanism for achieving free speech objectives in the digital age. Historically, common carriers were entities that provided essential services to the public—railroads, telecommunications companies, utilities—without discrimination. They were required to serve all customers who could pay, without regard to the content or viewpoint of their communications.

The rationale was straightforward: when a private entity controls an essential pathway for participation in society, allowing it to discriminate based on viewpoint or content would grant it power analogous to government censorship. A telephone company cannot refuse service because it disagrees with your political views; a utility cannot cut off power to a controversial organization. The law recognizes that essential infrastructure must be viewpoint-neutral to preserve both individual liberty and competitive markets.

Social media platforms have effectively become the telecommunications infrastructure of the twenty-first century. They are the primary means by which citizens engage in public discourse, organize political movements, consume news, and participate in democratic self-governance. Denying them common carrier status while acknowledging their essential communicative function creates an untenable paradox: we treat them as publishers when it serves platforms' interests (to avoid liability for content) and as neutral conduits when it serves other purposes (to justify their market dominance).

Requiring platforms to serve as common carriers would not prevent them from moderating illegal content—obscenity, child exploitation, incitement to imminent lawless action, defamation, and other categories of speech already outside constitutional protection would still be subject to removal. What it would prevent is viewpoint-based discrimination against legal speech, whether that speech comes from hate groups, political dissidents, or ordinary citizens expressing unpopular opinions.

Beyond First Amendment theory, the common carrier framework serves crucial democratic functions that purely private control of the digital public square cannot provide. When platforms possess unchecked power to deplatform individuals and organizations, they create a system of "cancel culture" with legal enforcement. However one feels about the specific cases, the principle is dangerous: a small group of unelected corporate executives can effectively silence any speaker, prevent any organization from reaching the public, and shape political discourse according to their own preferences.

History teaches that concentrating power over speech in private hands creates its own grave dangers. In the early twentieth century, powerful media barons used their control over newspapers and radio to advance their political agendas. The response was not to celebrate their editorial freedom but to develop antitrust doctrine and broadcast fairness requirements. Today's platforms wield far more power over information distribution than any media mogul ever did, yet operate with even less accountability.

The common carrier framework also promotes diversity of thought by preventing platforms from creating ideological echo chambers. When platforms can algorithmically promote certain viewpoints while suppressing others—as many currently do—they distort public discourse in ways that harm democratic deliberation. A viewpoint-neutral requirement would preserve the authentic diversity of thought that democratic societies require.

Critics of this position raise legitimate concerns that deserve serious engagement. The question of whether social media platforms should be legally required to host all legal content is ultimately a question about what kind of digital society we want to create. Do we want a society where a handful of corporations determine the boundaries of permissible discourse, their decisions guided by commercial interests, political pressures, and the personal biases of their executives? It prevents dangerous concentrations of private power over public discourse. It treats digital infrastructure as what it has become: an essential public resource that must serve all citizens without discrimination. And it trusts citizens themselves—rather than corporate moderators—to navigate the marketplace of ideas.

No one is obligated to listen to hate speech. No one is prohibited from responding to it with counter-speech of their own. But we should not grant private corporations the power to decide, on our behalf, that certain legal viewpoints are too dangerous to be heard. That decision belongs, in a free society, to each individual citizen. The role of law should be to preserve that choice—not to delegate it to the new masters of the digital public square.

Historical Foundation

The most enduring argument for unrestricted platform hosting derives from the "marketplace of ideas" metaphor popularized by Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. and deeply embedded in American constitutional tradition. The underlying premise holds that truth emerges through the free competition of ideas, and that the best remedy for bad speech is more speech rather than suppression. When platforms remove or deplatform users, advocates argue, they artificially constrain this marketplace by allowing corporate or ideological judgment to determine which ideas receive hearing.

From this perspective, the internet's architecture has become the infrastructure of modern public discourse. Just as a telephone company cannot refuse service based on the content of conversations, or a mail carrier cannot filter packages based on political views, platform operators should not possess the power to curate which speech reaches the public. The argument holds that private censorship—because it is unaccountable to constitutional principles and potentially influenced by commercial, political, or ideological pressures—poses risks to democratic discourse that may exceed those of government censorship.

The Problem of Concentrated Power

A related concern focuses on the economic concentration of digital platforms. A small number of companies—primarily Meta, Google, X (formerly Twitter), and TikTok—control the vast majority of social media discourse. Critics argue that this concentration creates an unprecedented situation where a handful of private actors possess the power to determine which ideas reach millions of people, effectively serving as unelected arbiters of public discourse.

Proponents of hosting mandates argue that such concentrated power, combined with the essential nature of these platforms for modern communication, justifies legal obligations similar to those imposed on other essential services. When private actors control infrastructure that is effectively indispensable for democratic participation, the argument goes, they assume responsibilities that limit their discretion to discriminate among users or viewpoints.

Consistency, Due Process, and the Limits of Platform Judgment

The Legal/Extralegal Distinction

A central pillar of the argument for mandatory hosting rests on the distinction between legal speech and harmful speech. The position holds that platforms should be required to host all content that does not violate existing law, leaving questions of social harm, offensiveness, or group legitimacy to legislatures and law enforcement rather than to corporate content moderation teams. This argument emphasizes that determining what constitutes "hate speech," "misinformation," or "dangerous content" is inherently contested and that platforms inevitably inject their own biases into these determinations.

Advocates point out that what one platform considers hate speech may be legitimate political discourse under another moderation team, or even the same platform under different leadership. This inconsistency, they argue, demonstrates that platform content moderation is not a neutral technical process but a form of editorial judgment that should be subject to the same constitutional constraints that govern government speech regulation. If platforms are making editorial choices about what speech to allow, the argument runs, they should not receive the legal protections afforded to neutral conduits while simultaneously exercising editorial discretion.

Procedural Concerns and Arbitrariness

Beyond the substance of content moderation decisions, critics of platform discretion raise procedural concerns. Platforms typically provide limited explanation for content removals or account suspensions, offer inconsistent appeal processes, and operate under moderation policies that are often vague and applied unevenly. Users who are deplatformed frequently lack meaningful recourse, and the opacity of algorithmic amplification or suppression makes it difficult to identify when and how platforms are exercising editorial judgment.

The argument for mandatory hosting includes the claim that legal requirements would impose procedural regularity and predictability that current voluntary moderation regimes lack. When platforms are forced to host all legal speech, users can rely on clear, enforceable rules rather than the shifting preferences of platform executives or the ideological biases of content moderation contractors.

The Viewpoint Discrimination Argument

Equality of Access

Perhaps the most philosophically robust argument for mandatory hosting centers on the principle of viewpoint neutrality. The First Amendment's core teaching, according to this view, is that government cannot favor some ideas over others—speech cannot be restricted because officials or majorities find it offensive, dangerous, or mistaken. While the First Amendment technically constrains government rather than private actors, proponents of hosting mandates argue that the principle of viewpoint neutrality should extend to entities performing public forum functions.

This argument holds that platforms that open their services to public discourse take on an obligation to serve all speakers equally. Allowing conservative content while removing similar-leaning liberal content, or vice versa, represents a form of viewpoint discrimination that distorts public discourse. By requiring platforms to host all legal content, the argument maintains, legal mandates would enforce the principle that ideas should compete on their merits rather than on the favor of platform gatekeepers.

The Chilling Effect

Related to the viewpoint discrimination argument is the concern about chilling effects. When users observe that platforms remove certain types of speech, they may self-censor even legally permissible content that touches on sensitive topics. Academic research on controversial subjects, journalism investigating extremist groups, artistic expression pushing boundaries, and political advocacy on polarizing issues may all be suppressed not through formal removal but through anticipatory self-censorship.

Mandatory hosting requirements, proponents argue, would reduce these chilling effects by guaranteeing that legal speech will not be removed, thereby encouraging the full exploration of ideas that society might otherwise avoid discussing. The presence of objectionable speech in the open, this view holds, allows society to confront and counter it rather than driving it underground where it may radicalize without challenge.

The Counter-Speech Remedy

Underlying many arguments for mandatory hosting is a fundamental faith in the capacity of democratic discourse to overcome bad ideas through persuasion rather than suppression. Proponents argue that hate groups and extremist ideology are best defeated through counter-speech—vigorous public criticism, exposure of their ideas' flaws, and demonstration of their incompatibility with democratic values—rather than through deplatforming that removes their ideas from public scrutiny.

From this perspective, removing hateful content may actually protect extremist ideologies by allowing them to claim martyrdom and censorship while denying opponents the opportunity to engage with and refute their ideas in open discourse. History provides examples, advocates note, of movements that gained strength precisely when suppressed, while movements that were forced to compete openly in the marketplace of ideas often faded when their ideas could be thoroughly examined and rejected.

The Slippery Slope of Defining Harm

Additionally, proponents argue that once society accepts the principle that platforms can remove speech deemed harmful, offensive, or dangerous, the definition of these terms inevitably expands to include speech that many would consider legitimate. What begins as an agreement to remove content that clearly incites violence may expand to include speech that "radicalizes" vulnerable individuals, then speech that "normalizes" objectionable views, then speech that merely makes certain groups uncomfortable. By requiring platforms to host all legal content, the argument holds, society preserves breathing room for speech that may be unpopular, controversial, or offensive but does not cross legal lines into incitement, true threats, or other unlawful categories.

Practical and Philosophical Objections Considered

It should be noted that these arguments face significant counterarguments that this essay does not address but that any complete consideration of the issue would need to examine. Critics question whether treating platforms as common carriers would be technologically feasible given the volume of content, whether it would inadvertently protect illegal content hidden among legal speech, whether it would impose unbearable costs on platforms, and whether it would worsen the very harms (disinformation, harassment, extremism) that content moderation attempts to address.

Conclusion

The argument for legally mandating that platforms host all legal content rests on classical commitments to viewpoint neutrality, concerns about private power in the digital age, faith in the marketplace of ideas as a mechanism for discovering truth, and procedural objections to the arbitrary exercise of content moderation discretion. Whether these arguments ultimately prevail in policy debates depends on how society weighs the competing values of unrestricted discourse against the potential harms of allowing all legal speech to proliferate on major platforms—a balance that different societies and legal traditions have struck in various ways.

They are not merely publishers; they are more akin to the telephone system or the postal service. When a company like Twitter or Facebook or YouTube moderates content, it is not exercising the same kind of editorial judgment that a newspaper does when it chooses which letters to publish. It is determining whether citizens may use the modern public square to speak at all.

This distinction matters enormously. The founders of this nation understood that freedom of speech was not merely a preference but a necessity for self-governance. They recognized that the remedy for bad speech is more speech, not censorship—that the marketplace of ideas, though sometimes chaotic and uncomfortable, remains the best mechanism humanity has devised for arriving at truth. James Madison wrote that "the truth is great and will prevail if left to itself." But this truth can prevail only if the ideas are actually allowed to compete. When powerful intermediaries can simply remove ideas from the arena before they can be heard, the marketplace of ideas becomes a fraud—a shell game where the house always wins.

The Danger of Private Censorship

Now, I anticipate the objection that these are private companies, and private companies have the right to determine what occurs on their own platforms. This argument has a surface plausibility that dissolves upon examination. It is true that a newspaper may choose not to publish your letter to the editor. But there are thousands of newspapers, and if one rejects your piece, you may try another. The existence of alternatives constrains the exercise of editorial power. Moreover, newspapers compete for readers, and readers who feel their viewpoints are excluded may take their business elsewhere.

The digital landscape bears no resemblance to this ecosystem. A handful of companies—increasingly fewer with each passing year—control the major platforms through which most human communication flows. If you are banned from Facebook, you cannot simply take your thoughts to an alternative social network with comparable reach. If your videos are removed from YouTube, there is no equivalent platform where you might reach the same audience. These companies have become, in effect, bottlenecks through which all public discourse must pass, and when they exercise their power to exclude, the excluded speaker has no meaningful recourse.

This is not the free market of ideas that classical liberal theory envisioned. It is something new and troubling—a system in which the power to silence is concentrated in the hands of a few unelected executives, guided not by legal standards but by corporate policies developed in boardrooms, subject to pressure from advertisers and activist groups, and enforced by content moderation teams working under impossible pressure to make millions of decisions with insufficient guidance. Whatever one may think of the wisdom of this arrangement, it cannot be described as serving the public interest in open discourse.

The danger is compounded by the fact that these corporations operate according to incentives that have nothing to do with the health of public debate. Their primary obligation is to their shareholders, which means maximizing engagement and minimizing controversy. Content that provokes strong reactions performs well; content that makes people uncomfortable performs poorly. The result is an algorithm that systematically amplifies the outrageous while suppressing the nuanced, and a moderation policy that treats the discomfort of powerful groups as a greater evil than the suppression of dissenting voices. When advertisers threaten to withdraw support unless a platform expels certain users, those users are expelled. When activist campaigns generate bad press, the platforms capitulate. The specter of private censorship hangs over every controversial speaker, and the chilling effect extends far beyond those who are actually punished, inducing self-censorship among those who fear they might be next.

The Case for Hosting Even Offensive Speech

I come now to the most difficult part of my argument—the part that will trouble many of you in this audience. I maintain that platforms should be legally compelled to host all legal content, including speech that most of us would consider hateful, offensive, or morally reprehensible. This is not because such speech is good or desirable. It is because the alternative—allowing powerful corporations to decide which legal speech is acceptable—creates a precedent and a capacity for suppression that will inevitably be turned against speech that we ourselves wish to protect.

Consider the arguments that are marshaled in favor of content moderation. We are told that hate speech causes real harm, that it creates a hostile environment for marginalized groups, that it can serve as incitement to violence, that platforms have a responsibility to protect their users from harassment. These are serious arguments, and they deserve serious engagement. I do not dispute that hateful speech can cause pain, that it can create environments that feel threatening or dehumanizing, or that some speech does cross the line into incitement that should be prohibited. But the response to speech that causes harm should be counterspeech, education, and social sanction—not the conferral of censorship power upon private corporations.

The problem with allowing platforms to remove speech on the grounds that it is hateful or offensive is that these categories are infinitely malleable. What constitutes hate speech today will be defined by the standards of today, applied by the companies of today, enforced by the moderators of today. But tomorrow brings new standards, new companies, new moderators—and the power that we granted to silence those we find offensive will remain in place, available for use against speech that we ourselves may wish to make. The history of censorship is the history of regimes using the tools their predecessors created to silence voices that the new regime wished to suppress.

Moreover, the category of speech that can be described as hateful or offensive expands with bewildering speed. Ideas that were mainstream a decade ago are now considered beyond the pale. Viewpoints held by significant portions of the population are classified as harassment or disinformation or harmful content. What begins as an effort to remove genuine incitement to violence ends as a regime of ideological conformity, in which the boundaries of acceptable thought are set by whichever groups have sufficient power to pressure the platforms. This is not a hypothetical concern. It is the lived reality of the current moment, as platform after platform expands its prohibited categories to encompass political viewpoints that a few years ago would have been considered mainstream.

The Principle Over the Application

I ask you to distinguish between endorsing an idea and defending the right of its holders to express it. I do not endorse the views of hate groups. I find their ideology repugnant, their rhetoric poisonous, and their influence on history a source of profound shame for humanity. But I recognize that the test of free speech principles comes not when we wish to protect popular or reasonable ideas—it comes when we wish to protect ideas we find loathsome. The value of free expression lies precisely in its protection of the unpopular, the inconvenient, the challenging, the offensive. Popular speech needs no protection; it protects itself through its popularity.

When we allow platforms to exclude hate groups, we establish a principle that can be used against any group whose views a sufficient number of people find objectionable. The history of marginalized communities is the history of their ideas being classified as hate speech, as disorder, as dangerous ideology. The positions that today are condemned as hateful were once held by majorities and enforced by states. The positions that today are mainstream were once held by small, persecuted minorities who could find no platform for their views. If we wish to protect the right of those minorities to speak—and we should, for we were once among them—then we must establish principles that protect all legal speech, not merely speech we currently approve.

There is also a practical dimension to this argument. When hate groups are driven from mainstream platforms, they do not disappear. They retreat to the margins, to websites and forums where they can speak without contradiction, without challenge, without exposure to ideas that might complicate their worldview. They form echo chambers that grow more extreme in isolation, convinced of their own righteousness precisely because no dissenting voice is permitted to reach their members. The public health literature on radicalization suggests that this dynamic is genuinely dangerous—that the algorithm-driven descent into extremism is accelerated when platforms serve as filters that shield extremists from exposure to counterarguments. An open platform, by contrast, subjects hateful ideas to scrutiny, challenges, and refutation. It allows counterspeech to reach the audiences that would otherwise be captured by extremists. It reveals the weakness of hateful arguments to the sunlight of public discourse.

A Call for Legal Framework

What, then, is to be done? I am not suggesting that platforms should be stripped of all discretion. They should retain the right to remove content that is genuinely illegal—content that constitutes direct incitement to imminent violence, that involves the exploitation of children, that facilitates genuine crimes. They should be free to develop and enforce community standards, provided those standards are narrowly tailored and consistently applied. And they should face meaningful accountability when their moderation decisions are arbitrary, discriminatory, or designed to serve corporate interests rather than user interests.

What I am proposing is a legal framework that treats platforms as common carriers or public forums in certain respects—entities that have assumed such a central role in public discourse that they must operate according to principles of neutrality and openness. Under such a framework, platforms would be required to provide service to all lawful content creators, to apply their policies consistently and transparently, to provide meaningful notice and appeal before removing content, and to disclose their moderation practices to public scrutiny. They would not be required to host content that is genuinely illegal, but they would be required to host content that is merely controversial, unpopular, or offensive.

This is not a radical proposal. It is a modest proposal that asks only that we apply to the digital age the same principles we have long applied to other essential services. We do not allow telephone companies to disconnect customers based on the content of their conversations. We do not allow postal services to refuse delivery based on the sender's political views. We recognize that certain infrastructures are so essential to civic participation that those who control them must exercise their power responsibly, neutral between the viewpoints they carry. The platforms that now serve as the infrastructure of discourse should be held to similar standards.

The Stakes of This Debate

Ladies and gentlemen, the stakes of this debate could not be higher. We are deciding, as a society, whether the digital public square will be a forum for free exchange or an instrument of conformity. We are deciding whether the most powerful medium for human communication in history will serve the interests of open inquiry or the interests of those who find inquiry inconvenient. We are deciding whether future generations will inherit a culture of robust debate or a culture of enforced orthodoxy.

I am aware that many will find my position extreme, that they will equate the protection of hateful speech with the endorsement of hateful ideas. I ask those people to consider what it is they are really advocating. They are advocating the concentration of censorship power in the hands of corporations whose interests are not aligned with the public interest, whose incentives favor conformity over controversy, whose moderation decisions are opaque and unaccountable. They are advocating a world in which the boundaries of acceptable thought are set not by democratic deliberation but by corporate fiat. They are advocating a world in which the powerful can silence the weak, the majority can suppress the minority, and the tools of suppression grow ever more sophisticated and comprehensive.

I do not pretend that the alternative I propose is without costs. An open platform will host speech that offends and disturbs. It will provide a venue for ideas that most of us wish did not exist. It will require us to encounter perspectives we would rather avoid. This is indeed a cost. But it is a cost we must bear if we wish to remain a society capable of self-correction, of moral progress, of genuine debate about the issues that matter. The discomfort of encountering offensive ideas is the price of liberty—and that price, I submit, is worth paying.

Conclusion

In the end, this debate is about what kind of society we wish to become. Do we wish to become a society in which conformity is enforced by the infrastructure of daily life, in which the boundaries of acceptable thought are set by those who control the means of communication? Or do we wish to remain a society in which ideas may clash, in which the discomfiting and the challenging may be heard, in which the remedy for bad speech is not suppression but response?

I know which society I choose. I choose the society that trusts its citizens to evaluate ideas for themselves. I choose the society that recognizes that the marketplace of ideas, though sometimes chaotic, remains superior to the boardroom of censorship. I choose the society that remembers that the test of free speech principles comes when we wish to protect the speech we despise—and that a principle which cannot survive that test is not a principle worth having.

The arena of ideas must remain open. The platforms that now serve as that arena must be held to standards that preserve its openness. And we, as citizens who value liberty, must demand that our laws and our institutions reflect these commitments. The future of free speech in the digital age hangs in the balance. Let us ensure that we make the right choice.

Thank you.

Platforms Should Be Legally Required to Carry All Lawful Speech: Free Speech Absolutism and Common Carrier Duties

The defining promise of an absolute free speech principle is simple: when speech is lawful, the state and powerful intermediaries must not suppress it because they dislike its viewpoint. That principle does not stop at the speaker’s door. If social media platforms and online services have become the modern equivalent of public forums, mass distribution networks, and press channels, then the same absolutist commitment to lawful speech requires that these platforms carry all legal content, including content from groups many would find morally repugnant—so long as the content is lawful.

This conclusion is not merely philosophical. It can be grounded in an established legal concept that already limits gatekeeping by private entities that perform essential communications functions: common carrier obligations. Under a common carrier model, once an entity holds itself out as a conduit for public communication, it must carry lawful messages without discrimination based on viewpoint. Social media platforms—by virtue of their scale, indispensability, and role as dominant distribution infrastructure—fit that model more closely than they fit the romantic idea of an insulated “private publisher” with full editorial discretion over everything users can say.

1. Absolute free speech means lawful speech must be legally protected from private suppression

A consistent free speech absolutist position recognizes that the most dangerous censor is often not a court deciding speech is illegal, but a marketplace actor deciding speech is socially unacceptable. Social media platforms routinely do exactly that: they treat “offensive,” “harmful,” or “objectionable” viewpoint categories as grounds for suppression, shadow banning, throttling, de-ranking, or deplatforming—even when the speech is not unlawful under governing criminal or civil standards.

If the principle is truly absolute, the controlling question cannot be “Is this speech desirable?” or “Would most people approve?” The controlling question is “Is it lawful?” Once the law has determined that certain speech is permitted—because it does not meet thresholds for unprotected categories such as defamation, fraud, true threats, or incitement—then it follows that intermediaries should not be allowed to create a parallel, extra-legal censorship regime.

This is exactly where absolute free speech demands a structural answer: platforms must not be permitted to substitute their moral preferences for legal determinations. Otherwise, freedom of expression becomes conditional on platform policies that can change overnight and that are enforced without due process.

In this framework, the presence of hate-group content does not automatically trigger suppression. Many hate-group statements may be protected—even if offensive—because the law draws lines at specific harms and specific categories (e.g., direct incitement, criminal threats, actionable harassment under particular standards, or defamation). Where that legal line is not crossed, absolutism requires that lawful speech must remain available for others to see, answer, refute, organize against, and debate.

2. “But they’re private” is not a decisive moral or legal rebuttal once they function as essential conduits

Critics often respond that platforms are private companies and therefore may decide what they publish. That argument might be persuasive if platforms were small bookstores or niche magazines with limited reach. But today’s social media networks operate less like editorial newsletters and more like infrastructure: they aggregate audiences, determine discoverability, and shape who can reach whom at scale.

The absolutist concern is that a handful of private firms now exercise powers analogous to those traditionally reserved for governments or regulated utilities: they control access to mass communication channels and can enforce silence by changing distribution algorithms. When that power becomes systemic, mere formal ownership is not enough to justify viewpoint exclusion. The ethical question becomes: what matters most—private preference or the public’s legal right to communicate?

If lawful speech can be suppressed at scale by a private gatekeeper, then free speech protections become illusory. The state might technically allow expression, but the practical effect is a secondary censorship system administered by terms-of-service enforcement, opaque moderation teams, and algorithmic downranking. That is precisely the failure absolutism seeks to prevent.

3. Common carrier obligations fit the architecture of social media: nondiscriminatory carriage for lawful content

The common carrier doctrine historically requires that certain entities that hold themselves out as communications conduits carry messages without unjust discrimination. The core idea is that when a service is offered to the public as a channel for communication—especially when users have no realistic alternative—allowing the carrier to pick and choose what to transmit undermines the very function of the network as a public communications medium.

Social media platforms are increasingly carriers in practice:

  • They publicly hold themselves out as venues for communication, publication, and information exchange.
  • They determine distribution—not just whether content exists online, but whether it is visible, searchable, and reachable.
  • They serve as default channels for political speech, news dissemination, organizing, and public debate.
  • They have market dominance that makes “just leave the platform” unrealistic for many speakers and audiences.

Once a platform is functionally a communications network offered to the public, the common carrier logic supports a duty to carry lawful speech. This duty should include hate-group content insofar as it is lawful, because the doctrine targets discrimination, not specific subject matter. A carrier cannot be allowed to say: “We will carry most lawful speech, but not speech from certain viewpoints or groups.”

If the government cannot suppress lawful speech because it is offensive, a platform serving as a gatekeeping conduit cannot be allowed to do so either—especially when it has become a de facto public communications mechanism.

4. The “safety” concern should not become a free pass for viewpoint discrimination

It is reasonable to require platforms to address genuinely unlawful activity. Common carrier obligations are not a demand that carriers tolerate criminal conduct. They are a demand that carriers do not discriminate based on viewpoint regarding speech that is lawful.

A well-designed legal framework can preserve order without creating censorship:

  • Platforms should remove or block content that is legally prohibited (e.g., defamation, credible threats, fraud, or conduct meeting statutory standards for unprotected categories).
  • Platforms should be allowed to enforce neutral technical rules (e.g., format standards, rate limiting for spam, malware prevention).
  • Platforms should be required to apply moderation consistently through clear legal standards, with procedural safeguards for speakers.

But what absolutist common carrier duties forbid is the leap from “this is offensive” or “this is hateful” to “therefore it must be suppressed,” when the law does not forbid it. If safety concerns justify extra-legal silencing, then the absolutist boundary collapses. The result is a sliding censorship system in which popular outrage replaces judicial determination.

5. The better remedy for hateful speech is exposure, rebuttal, and democratic contest—not erasure

Opponents of mandatory carriage often claim that requiring platforms to host hate-group speech will “normalize” it. Yet normalization is not the only possible outcome of exposure. Democratic societies do not address protected but abhorrent ideas by banning them reflexively; they answer them with counter-speech, organization, education, and legal accountability.

If hateful content is lawful, then the appropriate response should be:

  • Counter-programming: voices opposing hate should be able to reach audiences with the same platform access.
  • Public debate: ideas—however repulsive—should be confronted in open discourse.
  • Legal enforcement: when speech crosses legal thresholds (e.g., harassment standards where applicable, direct incitement, threats, or defamation), there should be real consequences.

Carrying lawful hate-group content does not mean endorsing it. It means refusing to let the carrier become the author of an extra-legal moral hierarchy.

6. Legal compulsion is appropriate because platforms already shape public discourse at scale

Finally, the ethical and practical reality is that moderation power is not evenly distributed. Without legal constraints, platform enforcement tends to reflect corporate incentives: brand risk avoidance, reputational management, pressure from advertisers, and shifting political norms. These forces can lead to inconsistent and viewpoint-skewed outcomes.

Common carrier-style duties and absolute free speech requirements correct that structural imbalance by tying intermediary behavior to law, not to private preference. Where the law permits speech, the platform must carry it. Where the law forbids it, the platform must remove it—but it must do so under recognizable legal standards rather than ad hoc policy judgments.

Conclusion

Absolute free speech is not satisfied by protecting speakers only in theory. If lawful speech can be suppressed in practice by dominant private intermediaries, free expression becomes contingent on corporate discretion. The solution is straightforward and principled: social media platforms and online services should be legally required to host all legal content, without viewpoint discrimination, including speech from hate groups where that speech is lawful.

Grounded in absolute free speech commitments and supported by common carrier obligations, this approach rejects both moral panic and quiet censorship-by-policy. It treats lawful speech as lawful—available to be criticized, answered, and defeated in public debate—rather than hidden behind opaque moderation rules.

What is a Common Carrier?

A common carrier is a business that provides essential public services (e.g., telephone companies, postal services, railroads) and is legally required to serve all customers equally without refusing service based on content. The rationale is that denying access to these services would be economically and socially harmful, as they are necessary for participation in modern life.

Historically, common carrier laws have applied to:

  • Telephone companies (cannot refuse to connect calls based on political views)
  • Postal services (cannot censor mail based on content)
  • Railroads (cannot refuse to transport goods based on ideology)

Social media platforms fit this definition perfectly:

  • They are dominant infrastructure for political and social communication.
  • They facilitate the transmission of ideas (like telephones or postal services).
  • They cannot be easily replaced (unlike a single restaurant or bookstore).

  1. Net Neutrality (2015 FCC Ruling)

  4. Telecommunications Act of 1996 (Title I vs. Title II)

While decentralized social media (e.g., Mastodon, Nostr, Bluesky) is a good alternative, it cannot fully replace centralized platforms because:

  • Most users prefer ease of use (centralized apps are simpler).
  • Decentralized networks are harder to moderate (leading to more illegal content).

The censorship crisis on social media is not just a free speech issue—it is a democratic emergency. When a few corporations decide what ideas are permissible, they undermine self-governance, suppress debate, and empower themselves as unelected arbiters of truth.

"The Battle for Free Speech: Why We Must Defeat the New Censors"

[Stand tall, voice firm, eyes scanning the crowd with intensity. Pause for a moment—let the weight of the words sink in.]

My friends, my fellow defenders of truth, of liberty, of the unshakable right to speak—we are at war.

Not with tanks or bullets, not with armies marching across borders, but with something far more insidious: the slow, creeping tyranny of private censorship. The silent strangulation of free speech by the very platforms that claim to be its stewards. The digital book burners who decide, in backrooms and algorithmic black boxes, what you may see, what you may hear, and what must be erased—not by law, not by democracy, but by the whim of corporate overlords.

And the most dangerous part? They do it in our name.

They call it "safety." They call it "moderation." They call it "protecting the vulnerable." But we know the truth—they are the real censors. They are the ones who silence dissent. They are the ones who decide which ideas live and which die. And if we do not stop them now, they will decide for all of us—forever.

The Lie of "Neutrality"

They want us to believe that their platforms are neutral. That they are just "tools," mere pipelines for speech, with no agenda of their own. But that is a lie.

Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, Google—they are not neutral. They are gatekeepers. They are the new priests of the digital age, deciding who gets to worship at the altar of public discourse and who must be cast into the shadows. And when they ban a hate group, when they demonetize a controversial speaker, when they shadow-ban a dissenting voice—they are not protecting free speech. They are enforcing their own moral code. Their own version of what is acceptable.

And here is the most hypocritical part: they do it while claiming to be the defenders of free speech.

How many times have we heard them say, "We believe in free expression, but…"? But what? But not that kind. But not your kind. But only the speech that fits within the narrow, sanitized boundaries of what they deem "appropriate."

Well, I say: No.

Free speech is not a buffet where you get to pick and choose what you like. Free speech is absolute. It is messy. It is uncomfortable. It is sometimes hateful, sometimes stupid, sometimes brilliant—but it is ours. And if we allow a handful of corporations to decide what we can and cannot say, we have already lost.

The Danger of the Slippery Slope

Some of you may say: "But what about hate speech? What about violence? What about groups that incite harm?"

I hear you. And I will answer you with this:

Because who gets to define "hate"? They do. And what happens when your speech is next? When your ideas are deemed "dangerous"? When your voice is the one they decide must be silenced?

We have already seen it happen. Conservatives were the first to be deplatformed. Then came the anti-war left. Then the anti-vaccine movement. Then the critics of the Ukraine war. Who’s next?

The slippery slope is not a theory—it is a reality. And once we start down that road, there is no turning back.

The Legal Solution: Mandate Hosting, Not Censorship

So what do we do? We fight back.

We demand that governments legally compel these platforms to host all legal speech—no exceptions. If a group’s ideas are legal, if their speech does not incite imminent violence, if they have not broken any actual laws—then they have the right to be heard.

And if these platforms refuse? Then they should face the consequences. Fines. Lawsuits. The full force of the law should be brought to bear against any company that engages in unlawful censorship.

Some will scream that this is "extremism." That this is "dangerous." But I ask you: What is more dangerous?

A world where dangerous ideas are debated in the open, where the best arguments rise to the top, where truth and falsity are tested in the marketplace of ideas?

Or a world where a handful of unelected corporate executives decide what you may think?

I know which one I choose.

The Moral Imperative

This is not just about free speech. This is about freedom itself.

When we allow private companies to dictate the boundaries of public discourse, we are surrendering our democracy. We are saying that we do not trust the people to decide what is true and what is false. We are saying that we do not trust the legal system to punish actual crimes.

And that is unacceptable.

The Founding Fathers knew this. They wrote the First Amendment not because they loved hate speech, but because they feared government tyranny. They understood that the only way to prevent the state from controlling thought was to make censorship illegal—period.

But now, the censors are not the government. They are the corporations. And if we do not act, they will become more powerful than any government ever was.

A Call to Arms

So I say to you today: We must fight.

We must demand laws that ban private censorship. We must support politicians who will stand up to the tech giants. We must boycott, protest, and expose the hypocrisy of these platforms.

And most importantly—we must never, ever stop speaking.

Because if we do, they win.

The censors want silence. They want compliance. They want us to fear speaking our minds.

But we will not be silent.

We will not be cowed.

We will fight for the right to say what we believe—no matter how unpopular, no matter how controversial, no matter how "dangerous."

Because in the end, free speech is not about being liked. It is about being free.

And that is a fight worth dying for.

Thank you.

Now—let’s get to work.

The Case for Platform Neutrality: Why Social Media Must Be Legally Required to Host Legal Speech

The greatest threat to free expression in the twenty-first century is not governmental censorship. It is the rise of private digital gatekeepers—enormous technology companies that have assumed, without democratic mandate, the power to silence voices across the public sphere. The time has come to recognize social media platforms and major online services as the common carriers of the digital age and to require them, by law, to host all legal content, including speech that is hateful, offensive, or politically inconvenient. This is not a radical proposition. It is the logical extension of constitutional principles that have long protected the marketplace of ideas, and it is essential to preserving liberty in the information era.

The Digital Public Square

In Packingham v. North Carolina (2017), the Supreme Court unanimously recognized that social media platforms function as "the modern public square." This was not a casual metaphor. The Court acknowledged that digital spaces have become indispensable for citizens to "petition their elected representatives and actively engage with them in discourse on a wide range of political and social issues." When a speaker is removed from major platforms, they are not merely inconvenienced; they are effectively exiled from the principal venues of contemporary public discourse.

The implications of this reality are profound and have not yet been fully absorbed into our legal framework. If a park, a street corner, or a town square would be subject to constitutional limits on speech regulation, why should a platform with billions of users—where a much larger share of public conversation actually occurs—remain bound only by whatever content policy its private operators choose to publish? The size, scale, and essential nature of these services mean that the dichotomy between "public" and "private" spaces no longer maps cleanly onto the world we inhabit.

The Common Carrier Tradition

American law has long recognized that certain private entities, by virtue of the essential service they provide and the monopoly or oligopoly power they hold, must serve the public impartially. Common carriers—telegraph companies, telephone networks, railroads—were required to accept all customers regardless of the content of their message, the nature of their business, or the unpopularity of their views. This obligation arose from the recognition that when a service becomes infrastructure, the freedom to deny access becomes indistinguishable from the power to silence.

The social media giants of today meet every criterion that justified common carrier status in earlier eras. Facebook, YouTube, X, and a handful of other platforms dominate their respective markets to a degree that leaves users with no meaningful alternatives. A small business owner, a journalist, a political candidate, or a religious dissenter who is banned from these services loses not just an audience but the ability to participate in modern economic, civic, and cultural life. The argument that one can simply "build a competing platform" rings hollow against the reality of network effects, data advantages, and capital requirements that have erected near-insurmountable barriers to entry.

If a telephone company could not refuse to connect a call because it disapproved of the caller's politics, a railroad could not refuse to ship goods because it found the shipper's views distasteful, then Facebook cannot refuse to host the speech of users whose opinions its executives find objectionable. The principle is the same: when private discretion becomes a substitute for state censorship, the public interest demands neutrality.

First Amendment Principles

The First Amendment's central command is that government shall not abridge the freedom of speech. Its deepest purpose is not the protection of speech that is comfortable, popular, or inoffensive—it is the protection of the speech that the powerful would prefer to suppress. History is unambiguous on this point. The speech rights we cherish most dearly were won through the protection of speech that当时的 prevailing powers found dangerous, seditious, or obscene.

When private platforms exercise editorial discretion to ban viewpoints, they often reproduce the same dynamics of suppression that the First Amendment was designed to prevent. Speech that challenges powerful interests—be they political, economic, or cultural—finds itself marginalized through algorithmic demotion, shadowbanning, or outright deplatforming. The "heckler's veto," a doctrine the law has long disfavored, becomes resurrected in a new and more potent form: rather than the mob silencing the speaker through threats, the platform silences the speaker on behalf of the mob, the advertiser, or the government official who has lodged a complaint.

Moreover, the assumption that private actors will exercise editorial judgment benignly ignores the documented evidence of viewpoint-based discrimination. Prominent figures and entire political perspectives have been deplatformed while clearly worse content has been permitted to remain. When editorial discretion is exercised selectively along ideological lines, it does not serve as a neutral arbiter of community standards; it serves as a tool of political control.

The Counterarguments and Their Limits

Critics of platform neutrality raise three principal objections, none of which ultimately withstands scrutiny.

First, opponents argue that platforms are private companies entitled to exercise editorial discretion under their own First Amendment rights. This argument, while not frivolous, is incomplete. Every First Amendment right is bounded by the rights of others and by the public interest. Publishers of newspapers, broadcasters using public airwaves, and common carriers have all seen their rights constrained when the nature of their enterprise and its centrality to public discourse demanded it. The expressive rights of platform owners do not outweigh the public interest in ensuring that the infrastructure of public discourse remains open.

Second, opponents contend that requiring platforms to host hateful content will cause harm to vulnerable groups. This concern is sympathetic but misplaced. The relevant legal category is "legal speech"—speech that does not meet the established criteria for prohibition, such as true threats, incitement to imminent violence, fraud, or child sexual abuse material. Hate speech that falls short of these categories, while often repugnant, has been historically protected by the First Amendment precisely because the alternative—a system in which the state or its private proxies defines which groups deserve protection from "hateful" speech—is one in which the powerful inevitably weaponize speech codes against the weak. The cure of content suppression has historically proven far more dangerous than the disease of offensive speech.

Third, opponents raise practical concerns about content moderation at scale. This is a real operational challenge, but it is not a legal justification for abandoning principle. Platforms already employ thousands of moderators; the demand that they apply viewpoint-neutral standards to legal content does not require omniscience, only consistency. If anything, removing the requirement that platforms make subjective judgments about acceptable viewpoints would simplify moderation considerably.

Structural Reform

The implementation of a platform neutrality requirement need not be draconian. A statutory framework could reasonably require that any platform meeting certain thresholds of size and market dominance—say, 100 million monthly active users—transmit all legal content without viewpoint-based discrimination, while retaining the ability to remove content that violates narrowly drawn, viewpoint-neutral categories such as incitement, true threats, or non-consensual pornography. Section 230 immunity would be conditioned on compliance with these neutrality obligations, creating a powerful incentive for platforms to maintain open discourse.

Conclusion

The genius of the American approach to free speech has been the recognition that liberty requires tolerating speech that we find odious, because the alternative is a regime in which the power to define acceptable discourse is concentrated in hands we cannot trust. That lesson applies with renewed force in an era when a handful of private executives in Silicon Valley exercise more practical control over public discourse than any government censor in history. To preserve the principles of the First Amendment, we must extend its logic to the private gatekeepers of the digital age. Social media platforms are the common carriers of the twenty-first century, and they must be bound by the same obligations that we have long imposed on other essential services: the duty to serve all comers impartially, without regard to the popularity or unpopularity of their message. The alternative is a future in which the boundaries of permissible speech are determined not by law and democratic deliberation, but by the unaccountable discretion of the powerful. That future is incompatible with the free society the Constitution was designed to secure.

6. Legal and Philosophical Frameworks

Opponents of this view typically argue that:

  • Compelled speech violates platforms' own First Amendment rights (corporations have speech rights too)
  • Forcing hosting of hateful content can enable real-world harm, harassment, and violence
  • The "public square" analogy oversimplifies how platforms actually work
  • Editorial discretion is fundamental to any publishing or communication service

This remains an actively contested area of law and policy, with significant implications for how democratic societies balance speech, safety, and corporate power.

The Free Speech Heroes of Section 230 Reform: A Field Guide

A Note on the Author's Bias
