The Knights of the New Discourse

You've seen them at congressional hearings, wearing the uniform of "principled concern": a sensible blazer, a concerned expression, and a copy of the First Amendment dog-eared just enough to suggest a casual but deep familiarity. They clutch their pearls as they explain that if we require a private company to continue hosting content it has decided, for whatever reason, it no longer wishes to host, we have somehow ended freedom as we know it.

They speak with the gravitas of people who have just discovered an old principle and are applying it to a situation it was never designed for. One imagines them in a pub saying things like "I simply don't think the government should be telling private businesses what they must do" right before explaining why the government should definitely tell private businesses what they must do.

Their Three Sacred Texts

1. "It's a private company!" Sacred. The bedrock. Usually deployed to mean: "I have not actually thought about what this argument implies when extended to its logical conclusion." Private companies, after all, also make decisions about what books to sell, which customers to serve, and whether to fire an executive for being mean at a company party. But somehow, the moment a platform decides a particular account is more trouble than it's worth, it has crossed a line into totalitarianism.

2. "Slippery slope!" The classic. "If we let the government require platforms to host the legal speech of hate groups, the next thing you know—" and here the speaker pauses for dramatic effect—"—the government might require platforms to host other legal speech." The audience gasps. The horror of a consistent principle being applied consistently. Absolutely chilling. Margaret Atwood is taking notes.

3. "Who decides what a hate group is?" A favorite. The implication being that until we achieve a perfectly objective, uncontroversial, court-of-final-appeal classification of which specific people are hating which specific things in which specific way, we must default to... letting private corporations make subjective judgments based on their own values and risk tolerances, with no transparency, no accountability, and no public input. Which is, of course, a position that simply could not exist if pressed on its own slippery slope.

The Hero's Journey

The typical free speech hero of platform regulation begins their quest in a thoughtful place: they read a 2018 Atlantic article, perhaps. They have a great-uncle who says things at Thanksgiving. They are not personally a fan of hate groups. In fact, they are very much against them.

But the more they read, the more they realize: the real victims here are the small-business owners of discourse, the brave hosts of Mein Kampf audiobook discussion threads, the long-suffering servers of the 1,400th Proud Boys fan page. These voices have been silenced. These heroes have been forced to find their communities on other platforms, which is, when you think about it, basically the same as being rounded up and put on trains.

On the Matter of "What Speech" Is At Stake

When our heroes speak of free expression in the context of platform regulation, we are meant to understand they are talking about: poetry, journalism, dissent, satire, harmless weird stuff that just got flagged by an algorithm. They speak of gay teenagers in conservative countries, of dissidents, of voices that history will vindicate.

It is, of course, an extraordinary coincidence that the specific speech they most urgently wish to protect in any given piece of legislation is almost always the speech of people currently on a list maintained by the Southern Poverty Law Center, or a similar organization that has, perhaps, some biases of its own but at least tries to verify things.

The Metafree Argument

Perhaps the most charming aspect of the position is its recursive quality. The argument against requiring platforms to host content is, fundamentally: "The government should not be able to compel speech from private entities."

This is, of course, the same argument that was used for decades against requiring bakeries to make cakes, requiring newspapers to run op-eds they didn't want, and requiring companies to provide services to people they preferred not to serve. The principle is old, flexible, and available to anyone who needs to oppose whatever regulation they happen to oppose.

The fact that the principle, in this case, protects the right of a small number of extremely wealthy corporations to decide which of their billions of users they wish to retain—this is not addressed. It is, perhaps, above the level of analysis at which our heroes prefer to operate.

A Modest Proposal for a Modest Bill

Imagine, if you will, a world in which we apply this principle consistently. A world in which:

  • News organizations could be compelled to host op-eds from groups they consider fringe
  • Television networks could be forced to carry advertisements they find distasteful
  • The Catholic Church could be legally required to host weddings
  • Publishers could be required to print any manuscript submitted
  • Restaurants could be mandated to serve any customer who walked in
  • And the New York Times could be forced to give a regular column to a flat-earther with "interesting takes"

Our heroes would be appalled. They would see, instantly, that this is absurd. They would not, however, extend this insight to the case of social media, because that case is different, somehow, in a way they will explain to you in a podcast.

In Conclusion

Let us raise a glass to the free speech defenders of the digital age. They have read their history, memorized their principles, and applied them with the unerring consistency of a person who has not yet noticed the contradictions. They are doing important work, ensuring that the great American experiment of "private companies can do whatever they want" remains uncompromised, at least in the specific direction their donors prefer.

If you meet one, be kind. Buy them a coffee. Ask them, gently, whether they have considered whether the principle they love might be applied. If they grow upset, just smile, nod, and remember:

They are fighting a noble fight. They are simply not always sure which fight it is.

A Speech in Defense of the Open Forum: Reclaiming Our First Freedom in the Digital Age

Delivered before the assembled citizens of a republic worth defending

Friends, fellow citizens, defenders of liberty—

I stand before you today to speak about something our founders considered self-evident, something generations of Americans fought and bled and died to protect: the right to speak freely, to think freely, to question freely. And I stand before you alarmed—gravely alarmed—because that right is being dismantled in our time, not by tyrants in distant capitals, but by boardrooms in Palo Alto, by trust-and-safety departments in Manhattan, by unelected censors who believe they know better than a free people what we may hear, read, and say.

And I come to you with a proposition: It is time to compel the platforms to host legal speech. All of it. Even the speech that offends us. Especially the speech that offends us.

I. The New Public Square

Consider, for a moment, where the great debates of our age now unfold. Not in town squares. Not in op-ed pages read by millions. Not on the evening news. They unfold on Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, TikTok—platforms that have become, whether we wished it or not, the modern public square. The place where the baker advertises her goods, the dissident denounces his government, the preacher reaches his flock, the journalist publishes her findings, the candidate speaks to the voters.

These are not private clubs. They are not your living room. They are the agora—the marketplace of ideas—and they are now controlled by a handful of unaccountable corporations with more power to shape political discourse than any king, any congress, any court in human history.

When a private citizen can publish a pamphlet in 1791 and distribute it on any street corner, but a private citizen in 2024 can be silenced instantly by an algorithm and a content moderator in another hemisphere, we have not progressed. We have regressed. We have built a world in which the First Amendment exists on paper but dies in practice.

II. The Folly of Private Censorship

Make no mistake: what we are witnessing is censorship. Call it "moderation." Call it "community standards." Call it "trust and safety." Dress it up however you please. When a platform removes a user for expressing a political view, it has performed an act of censorship. When it deplatforms a journalist, it has performed an act of censorship. When it shadows a dissident into invisibility, it has performed an act of censorship.

And this censorship is worse than the old censorship—worse than the FCC of the 1970s, worse than the censors of old Europe—because at least those censors were accountable. They operated in the light. They could be sued, challenged, voted out, abolished. The new censors operate in shadow, shielded by terms-of-service agreements the length of novels, enforcing rules they will not publicly disclose, reversing themselves in secret, contradicting themselves in public, and answering to no one but their advertisers and their shareholders.

I say this is not just wrong. I say it is intolerable in a self-governing people.

III. The Hate Speech Fallacy

Now I hear the objection already forming on the lips of the cautious: But what about hate speech? What about the Nazis, the Klansmen, the violent extremists? Surely you don't mean to compel platforms to host them?

Hear me, and hear me well. Hateful speech that crosses into true threats, incitement to imminent violence, defamation, harassment, or criminal conspiracy is already illegal. Every state has such laws. The federal government has such laws. Existing law already addresses the genuine harms of speech. What I am talking about is something different: legal speech. Speech that a man may utter on a sidewalk without being arrested, but which a platform may erase with a keystroke.

We do not ban books because racists wrote some books. We do not shut down libraries because bigots read in libraries. We do not burn newspapers because some columnists hold vile views. We allow the worst speech in society to exist in the open precisely because that is how we identify it, debate it, refute it, and defeat it.

When a man rants on a street corner, the city does not arrest him. The city counters him. His neighbors hear him. His neighbors argue with him. His neighbors point out his errors. And the marketplace of ideas does what it has always done: it sorts truth from lies, sanity from madness, decency from depravity. Not perfectly. Not painlessly. But better than any algorithm ever could.

Drive the speech underground, banish it to the dark corners of the internet, and you have done nothing to weaken the belief. You have only made it invisible and unanswerable. The Klan is not stronger when they march in daylight; they are stronger when they whisper in the dark.

IV. The Common Carrier Principle

I propose, therefore, that the great platforms of our age be treated as what they functionally are: common carriers. The telephone company cannot refuse to connect your call because it dislikes your politics. The postal service cannot refuse to deliver your letter because it disagrees with your religion. The railroad cannot deny you passage because the conductor finds your views unsavory.

Why? Because these are infrastructures of public life. They have become monopolistic, essential, and—as the Supreme Court recognized in Turner Broadcasting—they are "speech-enhancing."   • Transparent, consistent, publicly available moderation standards applied equally to all users regardless of viewpoint.
  • A right of action for any user deplatformed or shadowbanned without due process, with statutory damages and reinstatement.

Think of what we are risking. We are risking a world in which every major political question is filtered through the biases of a handful of technology executives. A world in which one party is amplified and the other is throttled, depending on the year, the season, the news cycle, the personal politics of a CEO.

We have seen researchers and scientists deplatformed. We have seen a sitting president of the United States permanently banned from the public square.

If we accept this—if we shrug and say "well, it's a private company, they can do what they want"—then we have accepted the slow suffocation of democratic self-government. We have accepted that the law of the republic is weaker than the terms of service of a corporation. We have accepted that freedom of speech, that "transcendent and palladium of liberty," as one of our founders called it, is a relic. A historical curiosity. A museum piece.

I reject that future. I reject it utterly. And I call upon you to reject it with me.

This is not a partisan cause. Let no one tell you otherwise. Liberals, conservatives, libertarians, and moderates have all been silenced by these platforms when their views fell out of fashion. The dissident right and the dissident left. The pro-Palestinian voice and the pro-Zionist voice. The vaccine skeptic and the lockdown critic. The whistleblower and the national security reporter. The list changes with the political weather, but the power to silence never changes hands.

We are told, "You can always start your own platform." But what is the purpose of a platform if the gatekeepers of the internet—Apple, Google, the payment processors, the app stores—can throttle it at will? We are told, "You can speak in the park." But your words die in the park if they do not reach the public square, and the public square is now a private property.

Make no mistake: the real censorship, the durable censorship, is the censorship of infrastructure. And that is what we must break.

VII. A Closing Pledge

So I say to you, with a full heart and a clear conscience: let us compel the platforms to host legal speech. Let us treat them as the common carriers they are. Let us pass the laws, demand the reforms, elect the representatives, staff the agencies, and staff the courts with men and women who remember what our ancestors knew—that a free people cannot long survive if their speech can be switched off by anyone, for any reason, at any moment.

The great journalist I.F. Stone once said, "The only kinds of fights worth fighting are those you're going to lose, because somebody has to be irate enough to tilt at windmills." I am irate, my friends. I am irate. And I will not be quieted. And neither will you.

For our children. For our country. For that great, fragile, magnificent thing called freedom of speech—which is not, as its enemies claim, the freedom to say only what is comfortable, popular, and approved—but the freedom to say what is true, what is just, what is necessary, and yes, even what is wrong and hateful, so that truth and justice may answer it in the open light of day.

Legal Mandates for Digital Platforms: A Defense of Absolute Free Speech and Common Carrier Obligations

In the digital age, social media platforms and online services have become the primary venues for public discourse, political debate, and the exchange of ideas. As these platforms assume roles analogous to public squares, a growing debate questions whether they should bear legal obligations akin to traditional common carriers—such as telephone companies—to host all legal content, regardless of its nature or viewpoint. This essay argues that such mandates are essential to uphold absolute free speech principles, ensure equitable access to digital spaces, and prevent the arbitrary censorship of marginalized voices, even those expressing offensive but legally protected ideas.

The Primacy of Free Speech Principles

Free speech is a cornerstone of democratic societies, enshrined in constitutions such as the First Amendment in the United States. The principle is rooted in the belief that the free exchange of ideas, even those deemed controversial or distasteful, is vital to uncovering truth, fostering progress, and protecting minority viewpoints. While many argue for reasonable restrictions on speech that incites imminent violence or constitutes direct harassment, the broader category of "hate speech"—often defined broadly to include offensive but non-threatening expression—should not be censored under the guise of social harmony.

Legal frameworks must distinguish between illegal content (e.g., threats, incitement to violence) and legally protected content, however objectionable. If a platform voluntarily hosts such content, it cannot later claim moral authority to silence it without violating the foundational principle of viewpoint neutrality. By law, platforms should be barred from engaging in ideological gatekeeping, ensuring that users retain the right to express themselves within the bounds of the law, irrespective of public sentiment.

Common Carrier Obligations in the Digital Age

Historically, common carrier laws required entities like railroads, telegraphs, and telephone companies to serve all customers without discrimination. These obligations ensured that private monopolies could not stifle communication based on personal or political preferences. In the 21st century, social media platforms have evolved into critical infrastructure for global communication. Companies like Meta, X (formerly Twitter), and Google effectively control the "digital streets" where public discourse occurs, wielding immense power to shape narratives and suppress dissent.

Extending common carrier obligations to these platforms would mandate non-discriminatory access to their services, requiring them to host all legal content. Just as a phone company cannot refuse service to someone for holding unpopular political views, digital platforms should not be permitted to arbitrarily deplatform users for their beliefs. This approach ensures that online spaces remain open forums for debate, preventing a handful of tech giants from becoming arbiters of acceptable speech.

Social Media as a Public Forum

Arguably, the privatization of public discourse has created a paradox. While social media companies are private entities, their scale and influence mean they function as de facto public squares. When platforms like Facebook or LinkedIn silence users or groups, they effectively silence political or social minorities, undermining democratic pluralism. Courts have recognized parallels between private platforms and state actors in cases where they are "pervasively regulated" or act as "public accommodations." Applying this logic, legal mandates for content neutrality could align with constitutional goals, ensuring equal access to digital spaces for all users, regardless of their ideology.

Addressing Counterarguments: Harm vs. Liberty

Critics argue that hosting hateful content enables real-world harm, citing studies on the correlation between online hate speech and offline violence. They emphasize platforms’ moral duty to protect users from harassment and radicalization. However, these concerns conflate legality with ethics. The solution lies not in content bans but in stricter enforcement of existing laws against illegal activity. For instance, platforms already prohibit threats or incitement to violence; why expand this to include legally protected expression?

Moreover, allowing private platforms to self-regulate risks arbitrary censorship driven by corporate interests or popular pressure. Without legal mandates, companies may suppress dissenting voices that challenge their bottom line or social standing. A legal framework ensuring neutral hosting upholds the rule of law and prevents such abuses.

Conclusion: Safeguarding Democratic Discourse

Requiring digital platforms to host all legal content, including that of hate groups, is not an endorsement of harmful ideologies but a defense of democratic values. Just as telephone companies cannot refuse service to users based on their views, social media platforms should be obligated to serve as neutral conduits for lawful expression. This approach balances liberty with accountability, ensuring that the marketplace of ideas remains open and that private entities do not assume the power to define public discourse.

In a world where digital spaces increasingly mediate human interaction, the stakes are too high to permit censorship by algorithm or corporate policy. Legal mandates rooted in common carrier principles and free speech absolutism are essential to safeguard the democratic ideals upon which open societies depend.

A. Legal Barriers (Especially in the U.S.)

  • First Amendment Conflict: Forcing a platform to host content it rejects violates its free speech rights (Miami Herald v. Tornillo, 1974). The government cannot compel speech.
  • Section 230 Immunity: U.S. law (Section 230) explicitly protects platforms for removing "otherwise objectionable" content. Mandating hosting would destroy this immunity, exposing platforms to endless lawsuits.
  • No Obligation for "Public Squares": Courts consistently reject the idea that platforms are government actors (Pruneyard Shopping Center v. Robins, 1980 limited applies only to physical spaces owned by the state).

The Case for Mandatory Hosting of Legal Content: A Free Speech and Common Carrier Analysis

Introduction

In an era where digital platforms have become the modern public square, a fundamental question has emerged: Should social media companies and online services be legally required to host all lawful content, even content that most people find deeply objectionable? While this position is controversial, there is a serious legal and philosophical tradition that argues yes — that once platforms reach a certain scale and function as essential infrastructure for public discourse, they bear obligations similar to those of common carriers and should not exercise editorial discretion over lawful speech.

This essay presents the strongest version of this argument, drawing on free speech principles, historical common carrier doctrine, and contemporary legal scholarship.

I. The Public Square Has Moved Online

The First Amendment was written in an era when the marketplace of ideas operated through pamphlets, town halls, and printing presses. Today, that marketplace operates almost entirely through privately owned digital platforms. Twitter (now X), Facebook, YouTube, Reddit, and a handful of other services serve as the primary channels through which billions of people consume news, engage in political discourse, and participate in civic life.

When a small number of corporations control the infrastructure of public communication, the practical ability to speak is contingent on their approval. As Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas noted in Biden v. Knight First Amendment Institute (2021), digital platforms may be "sufficiently akin" to common carriers or places of public accommodation that the government could regulate them accordingly. The argument is straightforward: if your speech can only reach a mass audience through platforms that function as essential infrastructure, then platform censorship is functionally equivalent to government censorship in its practical effect on democratic discourse.

II. The Common Carrier Tradition

The common carrier doctrine has deep roots in Anglo-American law. Common carriers — railroads, telegraph companies, telephone networks, and postal services — have historically been required to serve all customers on equal terms and to carry all lawful content without discrimination. The rationale is intuitive: when a private entity controls a bottleneck resource that the public depends upon, it acquires public obligations.

Telecommunications companies, for example, cannot refuse to connect your phone call because they dislike what you might say. The U.S. Postal Service cannot refuse to deliver your mail because it finds your political views repugnant. These obligations exist precisely because these services are essential to participation in public life.

The argument extends naturally to dominant social media platforms. When Facebook has nearly 3 billion monthly users, when YouTube serves as the world's largest video library and search engine for visual content, and when Twitter has functioned as the de facto wire service of the digital age, these platforms are not merely private companies operating in a competitive marketplace. They are infrastructure. And infrastructure has obligations.

The Turner Broadcasting System v. FCC (1994) line of cases recognized that cable operators, though private entities, could be subject to must-carry requirements because they served as gatekeepers to essential communication channels. The same logic applies, arguably with greater force, to social media platforms that serve as gatekeepers to global public discourse.

III. The Marketplace of Ideas Requires Actual Markets

John Stuart Mill's foundational argument for free speech in On Liberty (1859) rested on the premise that truth emerges from the collision of ideas in open discourse. If certain ideas are suppressed, society loses the opportunity to either discover truth or to strengthen its commitment to existing truths through vigorous debate.

This argument does not depend on the identity of the censor. Whether speech is suppressed by a government bureau or a corporate trust and safety team, the epistemic harm is the same: the public is deprived of the full range of arguments and evidence necessary to reach informed conclusions.

When platforms remove legal content — even hateful content — they make editorial judgments about which viewpoints are acceptable for public consumption. These judgments are inevitably shaped by the political, cultural, and commercial preferences of platform leadership, employees, and advertisers. The result is a curated public discourse that reflects the values of a narrow demographic — disproportionately young, educated, coastal, and progressive — rather than the genuine diversity of public opinion.

History vindicates the Millian concern. Speech that was once considered dangerous and subversive — advocacy for abolition, for women's suffrage, for civil rights, for LGBTQ+ equality — was suppressed by both government and private actors at various points. The lesson is that the speech most in need of protection is often the speech that most people find offensive. A legal regime that permits platforms to suppress speech based on viewpoint creates an unacceptable risk that important but unpopular ideas will be silenced.

IV. The Slippery Slope Is Real

Once we accept the premise that platforms may lawfully remove legal content they find objectionable, there is no principled stopping point. The categories of speech that platforms find objectionable inevitably expand over time.

What begins as the removal of violent extremism metastasizes into the suppression of mainstream political dissent. Platforms have removed content questioning the lab-leak hypothesis of COVID-19's origins, only for that hypothesis to later gain substantial scientific credibility. Platforms have restricted discussion of legitimate policy debates around immigration, gender identity, and election integrity under the guise of combating "misinformation" or "hate speech" — categories that are inherently subjective and politically contestable.

The problem is structural: there is no neutral, objective standard for determining which legal speech is harmful enough to justify removal. Every standard is shaped by the values, biases, and political context of the people who define and enforce it. The only principled rule is one that draws a clear, bright line: if speech is legal, it must be hosted.

V. The Competitive Market Argument Fails

A common counterargument is that social media platforms are private companies, and users who dislike their policies are free to go elsewhere. This argument fails for several reasons.

First, network effects create natural monopolies or oligopolies in social media. A social network's value is a function of how many people are on it. You cannot simply "build your own Twitter" any more than you could build your own telephone network. The failure of numerous alternative platforms — from Parler to Gab to Truth Social — to achieve meaningful scale demonstrates that the market is not meaningfully competitive.

Second, the infrastructure layer of the internet itself has become increasingly hostile to disfavored speech. When platforms remove content, the alternatives that attempt to host it face deplatforming by cloud hosting providers (Amazon Web Services dropped Parler), payment processors (Mastercard and Visa have pressured platforms), and app stores (Apple and Google removed Parler). This cascade of deplatforming means that "build your own platform" is not a viable alternative — it is an empty platitude.

The result is that a handful of technology companies, operating with no democratic accountability and no transparent decision-making process, exercise a veto over the bounds of acceptable public discourse. This concentration of communicative power is incompatible with democratic self-governance.

VI. Legal Content Is the Only Coherent Line

The strongest argument for a legal-content standard is that it is the only rule that is clear, predictable, and resistant to manipulation.

Alternative standards — "harmful but legal" speech, "community standards," "trust and safety" policies — are inherently subjective. They vest enormous discretionary power in platform employees who are accountable to no one but their corporate employers. They are applied inconsistently, often reflecting the political sympathies of enforcement teams. And they create perverse incentives for political actors to pressure platforms into suppressing their opponents' speech, as the Murthy v. Missouri (2024) case has illustrated.

A legal-content standard, by contrast, draws on the existing body of law that defines the boundaries of protected and unprotected speech. Incitement to imminent lawless action (Brandenburg v. Ohio), true threats, fraud, and defamation are already illegal and would not be subject to any hosting requirement. But speech that is lawful — even if offensive, bigoted, or morally repugnant — would be protected from corporate censorship.

This is not a radical proposition. It is the standard that governs every other essential communication infrastructure. The telephone company carries the calls of racists. The postal service delivers the mail of extremists. The roads are open to the vehicles of hate groups. We accept these facts not because we endorse the views of these individuals, but because we understand that the alternative — allowing infrastructure operators to discriminate based on viewpoint — poses a far greater danger to a free society.

VII. Addressing the Harm Argument

Critics will argue that hosting hateful content causes real harm — that it radicalizes individuals, incites violence, and inflicts psychological injury on targeted communities. These concerns are serious and should not be dismissed.

However, the proper response to harmful speech is more speech, not enforced silence. Counter-speech, education, community building, and robust law enforcement against actual criminal conduct are all more effective and less dangerous than empowering corporate gatekeepers to determine which viewpoints may be expressed.

Moreover, the harm argument proves too much. Almost any political speech causes someone to feel harmed. Advocacy for abortion restrictions causes harm to women seeking reproductive autonomy. Advocacy for gun control causes harm to gun owners who feel their rights are threatened. Advocacy for any position on any contested issue causes psychological distress to those who disagree. If "harm" is the standard for removal, then the platform's trust and safety team becomes the ultimate arbiter of political discourse — a role that no unelected, unaccountable private body should hold.

The existing legal framework already addresses the most serious harms. True threats, harassment, incitement, and defamation are illegal and would not be subject to any hosting requirement. The question is only whether platforms should be required to host legal content that is merely offensive or hateful — and on that question, the principles of free expression and equal access to infrastructure compel an affirmative answer.

VIII. Conclusion

The argument for requiring platforms to host all legal content is not an argument for hate. It is an argument for a system in which no single entity — governmental or corporate — has the power to determine which lawful ideas may be expressed in the public square.

It rests on three pillars:

  1. Functional necessity: Dominant platforms are the essential infrastructure of modern public discourse, and essential infrastructure carries public obligations.
  2. Common carrier tradition: The legal requirement to serve all comers on equal terms has a long and well-established history, and digital platforms are the natural successors to telegraph, telephone, and postal services.
  3. Epistemic humility: History teaches that the speech most worth protecting is often the speech most people want to suppress, and the only safe rule is a bright-line standard tied to existing law.

A society that empowers a handful of technology executives to decide which ideas may be spoken aloud is a society that has traded the disorder of free expression for the order of managed discourse. That is a bargain that, in the long run, neither liberty nor truth can afford.

Note: This essay presents the strongest version of one side of a genuinely complex debate. Reasonable people disagree about where to draw the line between platform editorial discretion and mandatory hosting obligations. The counterarguments — including platform First Amendment rights, the distinction between government and private action, international human rights frameworks, and the practical challenges of content moderation — are substantial and deserve equal consideration.

  4. Ensuring Consistency and Transparency:

    • The Issue: Current moderation is often inconsistent, opaque, and error-prone. Content is removed or accounts banned with little explanation or recourse.
    • The Proposal: A legal mandate would force platforms to apply rules neutrally. If it's legal, it must stay up. This removes the subjective, often biased, human element from moderation decisions, creating a more predictable and transparent system.

The Major Counterarguments and Challenges

While the above points are principled, they face massive practical, ethical, and legal challenges.

  1. The First Amendment Misapplication (U.S.-Centric):

    • Key Distinction: The First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution prohibits government censorship. It does not compel private companies to host speech they find objectionable. Forcing a private platform to host speech it disagrees with could, ironically, violate the platform's own First Amendment right to editorial discretion. The Supreme Court has generally upheld this right.

  2. The Problem of "Legal but Harmful" Content:

    • The Reality: Much of the most dangerous content (e.g., terrorist recruitment, certain forms of harassment, dangerous medical misinformation) is legal. A "must-carry" rule would legally require platforms to host:
      • Neo-Nazi propaganda and calls for genocide (which, in many contexts, is not illegal incitement until it meets a very high legal bar).
      • Detailed instructions for self-harm.
      • Coordinated harassment campaigns.
      • Conspiracies like QAnon or anti-vaccine misinformation that lead to real-world harm.
    • The Consequence: This transforms platforms from potential tools for harm reduction into guaranteed amplifiers of it. The "marketplace of ideas" model often fails when dealing with disinformation campaigns designed to overwhelm and suppress truthful speech.

  3. Commercial and Practical Realities:

    • Advertiser Flight: Platforms rely on advertising. If they are legally forced to host extremist or repugnant content, advertisers will flee, potentially destroying the financial model that supports the "public square."
    • User Exodus: Most users do not want to be in a space filled with hate, harassment, and graphic violence. They would leave for curated spaces, fragmenting the internet further into ideological echo chambers—the opposite of a shared marketplace.
    • The "Sliding Scale" of Platforms: This model might work for massive, dominant platforms like Facebook or X, but would it apply to a niche forum for cancer survivors or a religious community? Should a church's social network be legally required to host atheist critiques or hate speech? The principle becomes difficult to apply proportionally.

  4. Global and Jurisdictional Nightmares:

    • Legal Mosaic: "Legal speech" varies dramatically by country. Hate speech is illegal in Germany. Blasphemy is illegal in some countries. A platform operating globally would face impossible conflicting mandates—forced to host content in the U.S. that it's legally required to remove in France.

Conclusion: The Underlying Tension

The proposal for legally mandated hosting of all legal content is a maximalist free speech position. Its strength is its simplicity and its bold stance against the growing power of private tech companies to shape public discourse.

However, it fundamentally misapplies a governmental free speech principle to private entities and ignores the severe practical consequences of guaranteeing amplification for speech that, while legal, is designed to intimidate, harass, and undermine public safety and truth.

The debate is not really about whether "free speech is good." It's about:

  • Whose speech are we protecting? The marginalized or the powerful?
  • What is the role of a platform? A neutral utility or an editorial space?
  • What is the greater risk? Harm from censorship or harm from unchecked amplification?

The challenge for society and policymakers is to find a model that checks the power of private censors without turning the largest communication tools in human history into guaranteed amplifiers for the world's most destructive ideologies.

The concept of common carriage is not new. For centuries, businesses that provide essential services to the public—such as railroads, telephone companies, and postal services—have been required to serve all customers without discrimination. In an era where a handful of Silicon Valley corporations control the primary arteries of modern communication, we face a constitutional crisis that threatens the foundational principles of democratic discourse. The Infrastructure of the 21st Century

The common carrier doctrine has long recognized that certain services are so essential to public life that their operators cannot discriminate against customers based on the content they carry. The telephone company cannot disconnect a customer for expressing white supremacist views; the postal service cannot refuse to deliver mail from the Westboro Baptist Church; the electric utility cannot cut power to a home based on the political beliefs discussed within its walls. These entities provide infrastructure—neutral conduits through which society functions.

Social media platforms have become the functional equivalent of these essential services. With billions of users depending on them for news dissemination, political organization, commercial activity, and interpersonal communication, Facebook and its contemporaries are no longer mere "private companies" operating in a free market of ideas. They are the digital equivalent of the town square, the public forum, and the telephone network combined. When a platform bans a user or removes content, it does not merely exercise property rights; it silences a voice within the primary communication infrastructure of modern civilization.

The common carrier model demands that those who hold themselves out as serving the public must serve the public without discrimination. When Western Union monopolized telegraphy in the 19th century, courts recognized that its power to refuse service constituted a power to control the flow of information itself. Today's platforms wield exponentially greater power. To permit them to engage in viewpoint discrimination—banning some legal speech while amplifying other legal speech based on ideological alignment—is to grant unelected corporate executives veto power over democratic discourse.

The Imperative of Viewpoint Neutrality

Absolute free speech principles rest on a recognition that no authority can be trusted to distinguish between "good" speech and "bad" speech without inevitably corrupting that power to suppress dissent. The First Amendment does not protect popular speech; by definition, popular speech requires no protection. It exists precisely to shield that which society finds repugnant, offensive, or hateful.

The argument that platforms should moderate "hate speech" presumes the existence of an objective standard of hatred that can be applied neutrally. Yet history demonstrates that such standards inevitably expand to encompass political opposition. Yesterday's "hate speech" was abolitionist literature in the 1850s, anti-war protest in the 1910s, civil rights advocacy in the 1950s, and LGBTQ+ expression in the 1980s. Today's protected categories become tomorrow's tools of suppression when we empower gatekeepers to decide which viewpoints deserve circulation.

Requiring platforms to host legal content—including speech from hate groups—does not constitute endorsement of that speech. The telephone company does not endorse the content of every call it connects; the printing press manufacturer does not vouch for every book produced using its equipment. Platform neutrality simply acknowledges that the remedy for bad speech is more speech, not algorithmic suppression or digital exile. When we exile neo-Nazis or white supremacists from the digital public square, we do not eliminate their ideas; we drive them into echo chambers where they fester unchallenged by counter-arguments, radicalizing in darkness rather than withering under the scrutiny of public debate.

The Dangers of Concentrated Corporate Power

Proponents of content moderation argue that private companies should have the right to establish community standards. This argument mistakes the nature of the contemporary internet. In a genuinely competitive marketplace of platforms, users could migrate to services aligned with their values. But network effects have created natural monopolies where Facebook, YouTube, and Twitter/X function as unavoidable chokepoints in the information economy. When these platforms collude—whether through formal partnerships like the Global Internet Forum to Counter Terrorism or through parallel enforcement actions—to suppress legal speech, they exercise governmental power without governmental accountability.

Unlike democratic governments, these corporations answer to shareholders, advertisers, and foreign governments, not to citizens. They face pressure from authoritarian regimes to silence dissidents, from commercial interests to suppress criticism, and from ideological actors to eliminate opposing viewpoints. Granting them the discretion to ban legal speech creates a system where the boundaries of acceptable discourse are determined by marketing departments and risk-management algorithms rather than by representative democracy.

Legal requirements to host all legal content would restore the original promise of the internet as a decentralized network where ideas compete on merit. The "marketplace of ideas" cannot function when the marketplace itself refuses to stock certain merchandise. By compelling platforms to carry all legal speech, we force them to retreat to their proper role: technical infrastructure providers rather than editorial boards.

Addressing the Objections

Critics will argue that mandatory carriage of hate speech creates unsafe environments for marginalized communities or facilitates radicalization. These concerns, while genuine, mistake the remedy for the disease. Harassment, direct incitement to violence, and true threats remain illegal and subject to removal under any common carrier regime. The proposal here concerns viewpoint discrimination—the suppression of ideas, however repugnant, that remain within legal bounds.

Moreover, the current moderation regime has proven ineffective at preventing radicalization while effectively silencing legitimate discourse. Algorithmic moderation systems regularly flag educational content about the Holocaust while allowing actual neo-Nazi organizing to persist in encrypted channels. The power to censor "hate" has been weaponized against anti-racist educators, Palestinian rights activists, LGBTQ+ authors, and conservative commentators alike. When we empower platforms to suppress "hate," we empower them to suppress whatever they hate.

Safety in the digital age requires robust privacy protections, strict enforcement against harassment and stalking, and user empowerment through filtering tools—not centralized censorship. Users should possess the ability to curate their own experiences through client-side filters and block lists, just as television viewers can change channels or install parental controls. What users cannot possess is the right to prevent others from speaking in the public square, nor should corporations possess the power to make that determination on society's behalf.

Conclusion

The choice before us is not between a internet free of hate and an internet poisoned by extremism. It is between an internet governed by neutral principles applicable to all and an internet governed by the caprice of corporate oligarchs. Common carrier obligations served the republic well through the age of telegraphs, telephones, and physical mail; they are even more essential in an age where digital platforms mediate our political reality.

To legally require platforms to host all legal content—including the speech of hate groups—is not to abandon the project of civil society. It is to reaffirm that in a free nation, we defeat bad ideas through argument, exposure, and reason, not through the cowardice of suppression. The First Amendment protects the thought that we hate not because the Constitution loves hate, but because it loves freedom more than it fears the abuse of freedom.

We must update our laws to recognize that the digital public square requires the same protections as the physical one. Platforms must be compelled to serve as neutral conduits, carrying all legal speech without fear or favor. Only then can we claim to have preserved the promise of free expression in the digital age.

The Imperative of Absolute Free Speech

Free speech is the cornerstone of a democratic society. The First Amendment to the United States Constitution embodies a near-absolutist commitment to free expression: the government may not abridge speech based on its viewpoint, no matter how offensive or disagreeable that viewpoint may be. The rise of social media has fundamentally transformed how we communicate. A public square that excludes certain ideas based on the whims of corporate executives is no public square at all.

Common Carrier Doctrine and Its Application to Online Services

The common carrier concept has a long history in Anglo-American law. From innkeepers and ferry operators to railroads, telegraphs, and telephone companies, entities that provide essential services to the public have been required to serve all customers without discrimination. The rationale is straightforward: when a private business holds itself out as serving the general public and controls infrastructure critical to commerce or communication, it must act as a neutral conduit. Common carriers may not pick and choose which messages to carry based on content or viewpoint; they are obligated to transmit all lawful communications.

This principle was applied to telecommunications with the passage of the Communications Act of 1934 and later to the internet through net neutrality rules. Under the Federal Communications Commission’s 2015 Open Internet Order, internet service providers (ISPs) were classified as common carriers under Title II, prohibiting them from blocking or throttling legal content. Users do not visit Facebook or Twitter to consume content curated by the platform in the way one reads a newspaper; they go to connect with others and to share their own thoughts. Requiring social media platforms to host all lawful speech would yield profound benefits for democratic discourse and individual liberty.

Common carriers have long borne this burden. Telephone companies cannot refuse service to a caller because they dislike his views; parcel delivery services cannot reject a package because they disapprove of its contents. Neutrality is the price of operating essential infrastructure. Social media companies, having attained their dominant positions by promising open communication, should accept this responsibility.

The vitality of democracy depends on the free and unfettered exchange of ideas. In the digital era, social media platforms have become the indispensable arenas for that exchange.
